Weekly Corn and Ethanol Intel Report

Download reportPDFHTML
Week of September 3, 2026Market data through: September 2, 2026Narrative created: September 4, 2026Nearby corn: $5.188/bu (+$0.085 (+1.7%) week)

Weekly review of corn, ethanol, energy, co-product, policy, and related public-company performance for commodities risk managers at U.S. ethanol plants.

Strategy Narrative

Nearby futures from Yahoo Finance. Nearby corn is the market's current perception of yield and demand risk.

ContractLastWeek changeAs of
Nearby corn$5.188/bu+$0.085 (+1.7%)September 2, 2026
RBOB gasoline$3.104/gal-0.280 (-8.3%)September 2, 2026
Henry Hub$2.956/MMBtu+0.049 (+1.7%)September 2, 2026
  • 1. Corn held its risk premium as supply evidence diverged
  • 2. EPA finalized the exemptions, but not their full reallocation
  • 3. Gasoline futures weakened despite tight physical stocks
  • 4. Ethanol inventories finally drew, with exports providing structural support
  • 5. REX confirmed that physical crush and 45Z both contributed to profitability

Executive View

  • Corn-yield risk remained elevated but did not intensify at last week’s pace. USDA’s controlling August balance sheet still assumes a 180.7-bushel yield and 1.653-billion-bushel 2026/27 carryout, while Pro Farmer’s field-based estimate remains 173.2 bushels and 15.344 billion bushels. Corn condition held at 57% good-to-excellent, and a University of Nebraska model supplied a counterweight by indicating near-trend regional yield potential. Nevertheless, nearby corn closed at $5.188 per bushel, up $0.085, or 1.7%, for the week—a modest extension, not a reversal, of the crop-tour risk premium.
  • EPA confirmed a large refinery-relief package but deferred the offsetting demand repair. The agency exempted 1.76 billion 2025 RINs for 29 refineries. EPA had already incorporated 990 million RINs into its prior projection and said it would propose reallocating the roughly 770-million-RIN difference into the 2026 and 2027 obligations. The exemption is final; the incremental reallocation is not.
  • The petroleum price umbrella weakened sharply. Nearby RBOB fell $0.280 to $3.104 per gallon, down 8.3%, despite gasoline inventories falling to their lowest level in nearly ten months. High refinery utilization, weaker year-over-year gasoline demand and the early transition to winter-grade gasoline outweighed physical stock tightness.
  • The ethanol balance improved, but stocks remain heavy. Production edged down to 1.110 million barrels per day, inventories drew 171,000 barrels to 25.035 million, and EIA refiner and blender ethanol inputs rose to 940,000 barrels per day. Stocks were still 11% above last year, with Gulf Coast inventories 32.8% higher.
  • Export demand continues to prevent a larger product overhang. July ethanol exports totaled 199.5 million gallons, taking year-to-date shipments to 1.41 billion gallons, 13% above 2025. DDGS exports were also 13% ahead, supporting co-product clearance.
  • Overall margin and risk conditions deteriorated modestly: higher corn, slightly higher natural gas and an 8.3% RBOB decline outweighed the first weekly ethanol inventory draw in a month.

The week did not resolve the central corn question created by the crop tour. Instead, it added mixed evidence while the futures market retained and modestly increased its risk premium. Ongoing 45Z feedstock-documentation requirements and regenerative-ag carbon-intensity execution remain important but are not re-narrated absent a new federal rule.

1. Corn held its risk premium as supply evidence diverged

What happened

Corn condition held at 57% good-to-excellent for the week ended August 30, 12 points below last year. The crop advanced rapidly: 62% was dented versus a 56% five-year average, and 13% was mature, matching average. That reduces the remaining weather window and shifts attention toward harvest measurements. (USDA NASS, “Crop Progress,” August 31, 2026) (esmis.nal.usda.gov)

The University of Nebraska’s August 25 Hybrid-Maize simulations estimated regional yield potential near its historical trend, approximately 2% above trend in aggregate. However, the model excludes yield losses from flooding, nitrate leaching, disease, poor stands and hail—several issues relevant to this year’s crop-tour findings. (University of Nebraska–Lincoln CropWatch, “2026 Corn Yield Forecasts as of Aug. 25,” published August 2026) (cropwatch.unl.edu)

Demand evidence remains firm. USDA reported 475 million bushels used for fuel alcohol in July, 2% above June and 4% above July 2025. Corn export inspections finished the 2025/26 marketing year at 83.806 million metric tons, 25.1% ahead of the prior year. (USDA NASS, “Grain Crushings and Co-Products Production,” September 1, 2026; USDA export-inspection data, week ended August 27) (esmis.nal.usda.gov)

Why it matters

The new information does not validate Pro Farmer’s 173.2-bushel estimate, but neither does it restore confidence in USDA’s 180.7. With crop condition low, demand strong and corn up another 8.5 cents, the market is treating the September survey report—not late-season weather—as the next decisive evidence.

Risk-manager implication

Do not characterize national procurement risk as improving merely because condition stopped declining. The smaller weekly rally suggests urgency moderated after last week’s repricing, but harvest and winter coverage remain exposed to a USDA yield cut. Local basis risk will increasingly depend on early receipts and whether yield shortfalls overlap plant draw areas.

Watch next

Early harvest results and USDA’s September 11 Crop Production report.

2. EPA finalized the exemptions, but not their full reallocation

What happened

On August 31, EPA granted 18 full and 11 partial small-refinery exemptions for 2025, denied three petitions and found two ineligible. The exemptions cover 1.76 billion RINs. EPA said it would propose reallocating 100% of the difference between that amount and the 990 million RINs previously projected, split across 2026 and 2027, before the end of October. EPA also extended the 2025 compliance date to October 1, 2026. (EPA, “EPA Announces Action on 2025 Small Refinery Exemptions and Related Actions,” August 31, 2026) (epa.gov)

Why it matters

The action resolves the exemption package’s size near the upper end of the range discussed last week. EPA’s reallocation commitment limits the expected long-term demand loss, but a proposed future adjustment is not equivalent to an operative obligation. Timing, allocation between years and litigation remain relevant.

Risk-manager implication

The immediate exposure remains D6 RIN value and RIN-linked contract settlement, rather than a confirmed reduction in current physical ethanol blending. Plants should not assume that the roughly 770-million-RIN incremental shortfall is economically repaired until EPA publishes and finalizes the adjustment.

3. Gasoline futures weakened despite tight physical stocks

What happened

RBOB fell 8.3% to $3.104 per gallon on the supplied tape. EIA reported gasoline stocks down 1.2 million barrels to 205.7 million, approximately 6% below the five-year average, while refinery utilization increased to 98%. Four-week gasoline supplied averaged 8.9 million barrels per day, down 2% year over year. (EIA, “Weekly Petroleum Status Report,” September 2, 2026) (eia.gov)

Why it matters

The futures decline shows that seasonal supply and demand expectations overwhelmed tight inventories. EPA’s September 1 switch to winter volatility limits increased gasoline-production flexibility, while high refinery runs and softer consumption reduced scarcity value.

Risk-manager implication

The first transmission is through wholesale gasoline and ethanol’s relative blend value. Directionally, the move is bearish for ethanol selling and plant margins, even though cheaper pump prices may eventually support gasoline volumes. Plants should not expect tight gasoline inventories alone to restore last week’s petroleum-derived ethanol support.

4. Ethanol inventories finally drew, with exports providing structural support

What happened

EIA ethanol balance Week ended Aug. 21 Week ended Aug. 28 Change
Production, million bpd 1.112 1.110 −0.002
Inventories, million bbl 25.206 25.035 −0.171
Refiner/blender inputs, million bpd 0.923 0.940 +0.017

The national draw was driven by a 605,000-barrel Midwest reduction. East Coast stocks rose 340,000 barrels and Gulf stocks increased 133,000, leaving Gulf inventory 32.8% above last year. (DTN, “EIA: Ethanol Stocks Edge Lower on Week, Up 11% on Year,” September 2, 2026) (dtnpf.com)

July ethanol exports slipped 3% month over month to 199.5 million gallons, but year-to-date exports remained 13% ahead. DDGS exports totaled 1.10 million metric tons in July and 7.27 million year to date, also 13% higher. (Renewable Fuels Association, “July U.S. Ethanol and DDGS Exports Maintain a Steady Pace,” September 3, 2026) (ethanolrfa.org)

Risk-manager implication

Prompt ethanol exposure improved from accumulating surplus to heavy but clearing. Coastal builds caution against declaring the export channel tight, while the 1.110-million-barrel production rate remains high enough to support corn and limit rapid inventory normalization.

5. REX confirmed that physical crush and 45Z both contributed to profitability

REX American Resources reported fiscal second-quarter gross profit of $53.3 million, including $18.4 million of 45Z production-credit income net of estimated monetization costs. Management said core gross profit excluding 45Z increased 144% year over year. Ethanol volumes were flat at 70.6 million gallons, while average DDGS realization rose to $166.55 per ton from $143.63 and distillers corn oil to $0.72 per pound from $0.54. (REX American Resources, “Fiscal Second Quarter 2026 Results,” September 2, 2026) (investors.rexamerican.com)

The disclosure confirms that favorable co-product realizations and physical crush—not only tax credits—supported summer economics. Plant benchmarking should nevertheless continue to separate physical margin, accrued 45Z value and monetization cost.

Strategic Synthesis

The incremental thesis is persistent corn uncertainty combined with weaker gasoline linkage, partially cushioned by better ethanol clearance and strong exports. The corn market is no longer repricing yield risk as violently as last week, but it has not surrendered the premium. Until USDA reconciles its survey with crop-tour and harvest evidence, corn procurement remains the primary margin exposure.

What I’m Watching Next

  • September 8, 2026: USDA Crop Progress, delayed by Labor Day.
  • September 10, 2026: EIA petroleum, ethanol and natural-gas storage releases.
  • September 11, 2026: USDA WASDE and Crop Production.
  • October 1, 2026: Extended 2025 RFS compliance deadline.

Bottom Line

The week’s most consequential change was EPA’s final 1.76-billion-RIN exemption package, but the closest plant-margin exposure remains corn: nearby futures added another 8.5 cents while the USDA–crop-tour yield gap stayed unresolved. September 11 Crop Production is the event most likely to reset procurement risk and the overall margin view.

Company Overviews

Corteva (CTVA)

Crop inputs, equipment, and irrigation · $52.4B · 3m +15.6% · 12m +24.3% · 24m +61.9%

Google Finance

Largest U.S. corn-seed franchise (Pioneer) and a primary input cost for Corn Belt acres.

Corteva is an agricultural inputs pure play that was formed in 2019 when it was spun off from DowDuPont. The company is a leader in the development of new seed and crop protection products. Seeds generate the majority of profits with the remainder coming from crop protection products. Corteva plans to spin off its seeds business in late 2026. The seeds business will be named Vylor, while the crop protection business will retain the Corteva name and be a pure-play crop protection company following the divestiture. Corteva operates globally, but around half of revenue comes from North America.

Nutrien (NTR)

Crop inputs, equipment, and irrigation · $33.6B · 3m +16.7% · 12m +41.4% · 24m +72.9%

Google Finance

Largest North American agricultural retailer and a major potash and nitrogen producer.

Created in 2018 as a result of the merger between PotashCorp and Agrium, Nutrien is the world's largest fertilizer producer by capacity. Nutrien produces the three main crop nutrients—nitrogen, potash, and phosphate—although its main focus is potash, where it is the global leader in installed capacity with a roughly 20% market share. The company is also the largest agricultural retailer in North America and Australia, selling fertilizers, crop chemicals, seeds, and services directly to farm customers through its brick-and-mortar stores and online platforms.

CF Industries (CF)

Crop inputs, equipment, and irrigation · $18.0B · 3m +19.4% · 12m +64.3% · 24m +76.0%

Google Finance

Nitrogen fertilizer producer; corn is the crop that most moves UAN and urea demand.

CF Industries is a leading producer and distributor of nitrogen, which is primarily used in fertilizers. The company operates nitrogen manufacturing plants primarily in North America. CF also produces nitrogen in the United Kingdom and holds a joint venture interest in a nitrogen production facility in Trinidad and Tobago. CF makes nitrogen primarily using low-cost US natural gas as its feedstock, making the company one of the lowest-cost nitrogen producers globally. It is also investing in carbon-free blue and green ammonia, which can be used as an alternative fuel to hydrogen or as a means to transport hydrogen.

Mosaic (MOS)

Crop inputs, equipment, and irrigation · $7.1B · 3m +10.6% · 12m -21.1% · 24m -6.1%

Google Finance

Phosphate and potash producer that completes corn production budgets.

Mosaic is one of the largest phosphate and potash producers in the world. The company's assets include phosphate rock mines in the US and potash mines in Canada. Mosaic also runs a large fertilizer distribution operation in Brazil through its Mosaic Fertilizantes business.

Deere (DE)

Crop inputs, equipment, and irrigation · $156.7B · 3m +18.7% · 12m +48.7% · 24m +81.1%

Google Finance

Dominant North American farm-equipment maker for corn planting, harvest, and grain handling.

Deere is the world's leading manufacturer of agricultural equipment and a major producer of construction machinery. The company is divided into four reporting segments: production & precision agriculture, or PPA, small agriculture & turf, or SAT, construction & forestry, or CF, and financial services, or FS, its captive finance subsidiary. The core PPA business is the largest contributor to sales and profits by far. Geographically, Deere sales are 60% US/Canada, 17% Europe, 14% Latin America, and 9% rest of the world. Deere goes to market through a robust dealer network that includes over 2,000 dealer locations in North America with reach into over 100 countries. John Deere Financial provides retail financing for machinery to its customers and wholesale financing for dealers.

CNH Industrial (CNH)

Crop inputs, equipment, and irrigation · $16.5B · 3m +23.6% · 12m +21.7% · 24m +35.3%

Google Finance

Case IH and New Holland farm equipment serving corn growers.

CNH Industrial is the world's second largest manufacturer of agricultural machinery (82% of industrial net sales) as well as a major player in construction equipment (18% of industrial net sales). Its Case and New Holland brands have served farmers for generations. Geographically, agricultural sales are 40% in North America, 32% in Europe, the Middle East, and Africa, 18% in South America, and 10% in Asia-Pacific. CNH's products are available through a robust independent dealer network, which includes over 2,600 dealer and distribution locations and reach into 164 countries. The construction business leverages over 400 dealers. The company's captive finance arm provides retail financing to its customers and wholesale financing to dealers to maintain inventory, thereby supporting sales.

AGCO (AGCO)

Crop inputs, equipment, and irrigation · $7.0B · 3m +5.9% · 12m +17.4% · 24m +43.8%

Google Finance

Fendt, Massey Ferguson, and Challenger farm equipment with Corn Belt exposure.

Agco is a global manufacturer of agricultural equipment. Its main machine brands are Fendt, Massey Ferguson, and Valtra; its initiatives in precision agriculture have been organized under the PTx umbrella following a series of acquisitions. While a global business, Agco's sales skew heavily toward Europe/Middle East, representing 50%-60% of sales and even more of operating profits. The company is trying to increase its exposure to the larger North and South American markets. Its products are available through a global dealer network, which includes over 3,000 dealers and distribution locations and reaches into over 140 countries. Additionally, Agco offers retail and wholesale financing to customers through its partnership with Rabobank of the Netherlands, having exited their JV in 2026.

Valmont Industries (VMI)

Crop inputs, equipment, and irrigation · $9.3B · 3m -15.2% · 12m +26.3% · 24m +67.7%

Google Finance

Center-pivot irrigation (Valley) used on irrigated High Plains corn.

Valmont Industries Inc, along with its subsidiaries, operates as a manufacturer of products and services for infrastructure and agriculture markets. Its reportable segments are Infrastructure and Agriculture. The company generates maximum revenue from the Infrastructure segment, which includes the manufacturing and distribution of products and solutions to serve the infrastructure markets of utility, solar, lighting, transportation, and telecommunications, along with coatings services to protect metal products. The Agriculture segment provides irrigation equipment components, including aftermarket parts and tubular products, and technology solutions for precision agriculture.
